## The six framing scales {#six-ways-to-say-eu-framing .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Methods tutorial, 12 slides – skip to Hands-on 4 →](#hands-on-4-work-the-menu)
:::

::: {.small}
| Scale | Items | Claim predicts | Curve |
|:-----|:-------------------------|:--------|:--------|
| `mcosmo` | peace, democracy, free movement, diversity, voice | negative | the claim |
| `mutil` | prosperity, social protection | negative | the claim |
| `mcomm` | unemployment, identity, crime, borders | **positive** | negative |
| `mlib` | bureaucracy, waste of money | **positive** | negative |
| `mpos` | all seven positive items | negative | the claim |
| `mneg` | all six negative items | **positive** | negative |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The claim says "decrease positive dimensions": its curve holds the three positive scales, `mpos` the most literal reading and `mcosmo` the one instructed, and the negative scales have a curve of their own. On the curve of the claim the frame set carries **`r fmt_pct(fork_of("outcome"))`** of the variance and changes the class of **`r fmt_pct(fork_of("outcome", "crossing_rate"))`** of the pairs.
:::

::: notes
The outcome comes first. The survey question offers fourteen meanings, of which the paper sets the euro aside and sorts the other thirteen into four scales, cosmopolitan, utilitarian, communitarian and libertarian, and two composites take all the positive items and all the negative ones. The third column often causes confusion, because for the negative framings the claim predicts a positive coefficient. [advance] Since the claim speaks of positive dimensions, its curve keeps the three positive scales, and the negative scales have a curve of their own, because they test the other half of the hypothesis rather than offering another reading of this half. On the curve, the choice among the three positive scales accounts for about a tenth of the variation, and it changes whether a result clears the CR2 test in about a third of the pairs of specifications that differ only in the scale. The communitarian scale contains the item 'unemployment', which ties that outcome to the predictor by its content.
:::

## Building a scale – mean, sum or share {#building-a-scale-mean-sum-or-share .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Five binary items per respondent. Three defensible summaries:

- **Mean** of the five – a proportion between 0 and 1. Everyone contributes equally
- **Sum** – a count from 0 to 5. The same information on a different scale, which changes the size of the coefficient
- **Share** of all mentions – depends on how many options the respondent picked overall
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A **share** is relative to the respondent's own total, so somebody who ticked eight boxes contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. The mean and the sum do not depend on that total.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Among the five analysts of the robustness study, one used a **mean**, one a **sum**, one a **share** and one three separate shares. Each choice is defensible, but no two of them measure the same quantity.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The curve keeps the **share**, as the paper scores it. Scored as a count, `r fmt_pct(dev_of("count"))` of the curve specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r fmt_pct(share_sig(spec_curve))` as shares: a count measures how much a person says about the EU, which is another quantity.
:::

::: notes
Five binary items can be summarised in three defensible ways. The mean gives a proportion between nought and one, with every item counting equally, and the sum gives a count from nought to five, the same information on another scale, so that its coefficient is five times larger and means the same. The share of all the mentions of a respondent, which our panel uses, is relative to how many options that respondent picked overall. [advance] Somebody who ticked eight options therefore contributes differently from somebody who ticked two, which is not true of the mean or the sum. [advance] Among the five of us, one used a mean, one a sum, one a share and one three separate shares, all defensible, and no two of them the same quantity. [advance] The curve keeps the share, as the paper scores the scales. Scored as a count, the share of specifications below zero with a CR2 p under point zero five falls from about seventy-seven per cent to about fifty-one, because a count measures how much a person says about the EU, which differs from how that person frames it.
:::

## Claim alignment {#claim-alignment-and-why-the-room-needs-it .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.fs-95}
```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3"}
d <- d |> datawizard::data_modify(mcomm_ca = 1 - mcomm)   # reverse-code a negative framing

# now: negative coefficient = supports the claim, whatever the outcome
```
:::

::: {.small}
Reverse-coding a bounded scale **flips the sign** of *b*, *t* and *r*, and leaves the magnitude, the standard error, the |t| and the p-value untouched. The same holds exactly for the beta family, since logit(1 − μ) = −logit(μ).
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your evidence stays the same, and only the sign convention in which it is reported changes.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
It is still an analytic decision, so it is set by an explicit `claim_align` switch in your preregistration. On the curve of the claim every scale is positive, so the flip that remains is the one for GDP growth; the negative scales, reverse-coded, have a curve of their own.
:::

::: notes
Claim alignment, one of the ground rules of the menu, keeps the class chart readable. For a negative framing the scale is reverse-coded before fitting, as one minus the scale, which flips the sign of the coefficient, the t and the partial r and leaves the magnitude, the standard error, the absolute t and the p-value as they were. This holds exactly for the beta family too, because the logit of one minus mu is minus the logit of mu. [advance] The evidence stays the same, and only the direction in which it is reported changes. [advance] It remains an analytic decision, which a reader should be able to find, so it is set by a visible switch, `claim_align`, in your preregistration block. On the curve of the claim every scale is a positive framing, so the flip that remains in practice is the one for growth, and the negative scales, reverse-coded, have their own curve on the results page.
:::

## A bounded scale in a linear model {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Our outcome is a proportion. It lies strictly between 0 and 1, and its variance is smallest near the ends. A linear model assumes neither of those things.

- **Gaussian** – fit it as if it were unbounded. Simple and familiar, but it can in principle predict values outside 0–1
- **Beta** – a logit-link beta regression, built for bounded outcomes of this kind. It reports a **z** in place of a *t*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Fitted as a beta regression, the reproduced specification gives **r = `r fmt_num(beta_ref$r_ca_dev)`**, against **r = `r fmt_num(curve_ref$r_ca)`** from the linear fit, and its clustered test gives p = `r fmt_num(beta_ref$p_dev)`, against `r fmt_num(curve_ref$p_cr1)` for the same test of the linear fit.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Across the curve, `r fmt_pct(dev_of("beta"))` of the beta twins lie below zero with clustered p < 0.05, against `r fmt_pct(share_sig(spec_curve, spec_curve$p_cr1))` of the linear specifications under the same test. The curve keeps the linear model, and the beta family serves as a check of functional form.
:::

::: notes
Our outcome is a proportion, which lies strictly between nought and one and whose variance is necessarily smallest near the two ends, since a mean near zero cannot vary much, and a linear model assumes neither property. A Gaussian model treats the outcome as unbounded, which is simple and familiar and could in principle predict a framing score of one point two, while a beta regression with a logit link is built for bounded outcomes of this kind and reports a z in place of a t. [advance] On this claim the two agree. The beta version of the reproduced specification gives a partial r of minus point two six, against minus point two four from the linear fit, and under errors clustered by country its p-value is point zero two six, against point zero two nine for the linear fit under the same test. [advance] Across the whole curve the beta twins clear that clustered test about as often as the linear specifications do, so the curve keeps the linear model, which every analyst fitted, and the beta family stays on the menu as a check of functional form.
:::

## The predictor – unemployment or GDP growth {#which-variable-carries-the-claim .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
The abstract says "poor economic performances". That names at least two things:

- **Unemployment rate** – what Task 2 of the robustness study instructed. Higher is worse
- **GDP growth** – what four of the five analysts used in their free phase, two of them beside unemployment. Higher is *better*, so the claim predicts a **positive** coefficient on positive framings
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Refitted on our panel, the free-phase model of analyst C6HJR (`mpos ~ growth + unemp`, two-way fixed effects) puts the growth coefficient at **b = +`r fmt_num(growth_c6hjr$b, 5)`, t = `r fmt_num(growth_c6hjr$t, 2)`**, CR2 p = `r fmt_num(growth_c6hjr$p_cr2)`: in the direction predicted by the claim but not significant.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Across the `r nrow(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, predictor == "growth"))` growth specifications on the curve, **`r fmt_pct(share_below(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, predictor == "growth")))`** point in the direction predicted by the claim, but only **`r fmt_pct(share_sig(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, predictor == "growth")))`** lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r fmt_pct(share_sig(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, predictor == "unemp")))` of the `r nrow(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, predictor == "unemp"))` unemployment specifications. Direction without significance is a different kind of support.
:::

::: notes
The abstract says "poor economic performances", a phrase that names at least two things. One is the unemployment rate, which the robustness study instructed in its second task and for which higher means worse. The other is GDP growth, which four of the five of us used when we were free to choose and for which higher means better, so that the claim predicts a positive coefficient on the positive framings. [advance] My own free-phase model, refitted on this panel with the positive framings on growth and unemployment and two-way fixed effects, puts the growth coefficient at plus point zero zero one seven, with a t of one point six and a CR2 p of about point three five, in the predicted direction and not significant. [advance] Across the ninety-six growth specifications on the curve, more than four in five point in the direction predicted by the claim, but only a third lie below zero with a CR2 p under point zero five, against more than four in five of the unemployment specifications. Direction without significance is a different kind of support, and a reader should be told which kind is on offer.
:::

## Predictor form {#predictor-form-and-a-warning .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- **Raw** `unemp` – a one-point rise in the rate
- **log(unemp)** – a proportional rise, so the step from 4% to 5% counts for more than the step from 20% to 21%
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Those two are genuinely different models and can give different answers: on the curve, switching the form changes the class of `r fmt_pct(fork_of("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, while carrying almost none of the variance.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
But **centring and standardising are not**. Subtracting a mean, or dividing by a standard deviation, is an *affine* change of scale: it moves the coefficient and its standard error by the same factor and leaves **t, r and p exactly unchanged**.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
For that reason the curve has no separate centred rows. A robustness check that varies only the centring is the same analysis restated.
:::

::: notes
Raw unemployment asks what a rise of one point in the rate does, and logged unemployment what a proportional rise does, which is a different claim, since it makes the step from four per cent to five matter more than the step from twenty to twenty-one, a plausible assumption, I think, for unemployment. [advance] The two forms are different models and can give different answers: on the curve the form barely moves the estimates on average, yet switching it changes whether the CR2 test is passed in about one pair in thirty. [advance] Centring and standardising, by contrast, are affine changes of scale, which move the coefficient and its standard error by the same factor and leave the t, the partial r and the p-value untouched. [advance] Our curve therefore contains no separate centred rows, and a robustness check that varies only the centring restates the same analysis.
:::

## Estimators for countries and years {#four-ways-to-handle-countries-and-years .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
| Estimator | What it compares | Curve |
|:-------|:--------------------------|:-----------|
| **Two-way FE** | each country with itself, net of the change shared in a year | on |
| **Country FE** | each country with itself, shared change included | on |
| **Pooled OLS** | countries with each other *and* over time | off – another question |
| **Random effects** | a blend of both, assuming country effects unrelated to the predictor | off – fails here |
| **Within–between** | the two comparisons, separately | off – a check |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The two designs on the curve are two estimands. Below zero with CR2 p < 0.05: `r fmt_pct(share_sig(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, estimator == "fe_country")))` of the country FE and `r fmt_pct(share_sig(dplyr::filter(spec_curve, estimator == "fe_twoway")))` of the two-way specifications.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Across the 27 country means the cosmopolitan slope is +`r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$b_between, 4)`, within countries `r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$b_within, 4)`, and the within–between model rejects their equality (p = `r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$p_difference)`). Swapped in, pooled OLS leaves `r fmt_pct(dev_of("pooled_cl"))` of the twins below zero with p < 0.05.
:::

::: notes
These estimators do not answer the same question. Two-way fixed effects compare each country with itself and remove whatever all of Europe went through in a given year, and country fixed effects compare each country with itself over time and keep that shared change in. Pooled OLS compares countries with each other and with themselves at once, random effects blend the two comparisons and assume that stable differences between countries are unrelated to unemployment, and the within–between model estimates the two comparisons separately, which lets us check that assumption. [advance] The curve keeps the two fixed-effects designs as two estimands rather than two ways of estimating one, which is why the shares of their specifications that clear the CR2 test differ so much. [advance] Between countries the association has the opposite sign, since countries with high unemployment give slightly more weight to the cosmopolitan meanings of the EU, although that slope alone is not significant. The within–between model rejects the equality that random effects assume, and pooled OLS, which mixes the two comparisons, leaves fewer than one twin in ten below zero with a p under point zero five.
:::

## What fixed effects adjust for {#what-fixed-effects-actually-buy-you .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
**Absorbed**

- Anything stable about a country over the decade – institutions, history, size, prior EU sentiment
- Anything common to a year across all countries – the crisis itself, a treaty, a media cycle
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
**Not addressed**

- A confounder that **varies within a country over time** – a national bailout, a change of government
- **Reverse causation**: today's framing moving tomorrow's unemployment
- Measurement error, selection into the sample
- **The years of one country resembling each other** – a matter for the test, not the estimate, which is why the curve uses errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the same statement as the DAG from Hands-on 2. `adjustmentSets()` on its solid part, before any of the pale nodes is wired in, returns country and year, which are what two-way fixed effects absorb, so **the graph and the reproduced model make the same claim.**
:::

::: notes
Fixed effects are often treated as a general remedy for confounding, so I want to be precise about what they adjust for. They absorb anything stable about a country across the decade, its institutions, history and size or what it already thought of the EU in 2004, and anything common to a year across all countries, such as the crisis itself, a treaty or a Europe-wide media cycle. They do not touch anything that varies within a country over time, where the most interesting confounders lie, such as a national bailout programme or a change of government, and they do nothing about reverse causation, measurement error or selection. The last item on the right concerns the test rather than the estimate: the years of one country resemble each other, so conventional errors overstate the evidence, and the curve tests every slope with errors clustered by country, under the CR2 correction. [advance] On the solid part of the graph from Hands-on 2, before any pale node is wired in, `adjustmentSets()` returns country and year, so the graph and the reproduced model make the same claim.
:::

## The copredictor {#copredictor-control-or-second-exposure .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Put GDP growth in beside unemployment and you have made a choice you should be able to name:

- **As a confounder** – a slump raises unemployment *and* sours sentiment in the same year. Adjusting closes a back-door path that your fixed effects leave open
- **As a rival exposure** – growth is a second measure of the same "poor economic performance". Now you are asking which of the two the claim is about
- **As a mediator** – if unemployment works *through* growth, adjusting removes part of the effect you wanted
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The line of code is the same in all three cases, but each reading of it targets a different estimand. And remember the **Table 2 fallacy**, which is to read every coefficient in a regression table as a causal effect. The growth coefficient in that model is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

::: notes
The copredictor looks like the most innocuous choice on the menu, and it is easy to get wrong, because adding GDP growth beside unemployment is a choice that you should be able to name. You may mean growth as a confounder, a slump that raises unemployment and sours sentiment in the same year, so that adjusting for it closes a back-door path which fixed effects cannot reach, since growth varies within a country over time. You may mean it as a rival exposure, another measure of the same poor economic performance, in which case you are asking which of the two the claim is about. Or, if unemployment works partly through growth, growth is a mediator, and adjusting for it removes part of the effect that you set out to measure. [advance] The line of code is the same, and the three readings target three different estimands, while the growth coefficient in that model, by the Table 2 fallacy, is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

## Sample restrictions {#sample-which-countries-which-years .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- **All** – 2004–2013, 27 countries, 270 cells: the only sample on the curve
- **2004–2008** or **2009–2013** – the earlier window holds no crisis, and the later one drops the comparison with the years before it
- **Without the bailout countries** or **without Greece and Spain** – a population without the cases that the claim is most about
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
| The reproduced specification on | Slope | CR2 p |
|---|--:|--:|
| all 270 country-years | `r fmt_num(period_of("all", "b"), 5)` | `r fmt_num(period_of("all", "p_cr2"), 4)` |
| 2004–2008 | `r fmt_num(period_of("y2004_2008", "b"), 5)` | `r fmt_num(period_of("y2004_2008", "p_cr2"))` |
| 2009–2013 | `r fmt_num(period_of("y2009_2013", "b"), 5)` | `r fmt_num(period_of("y2009_2013", "p_cr2"))` |
| the 8 bailout countries | `r fmt_num(bailout_of("bailout", "b"), 5)` | `r fmt_num(bailout_of("bailout", "p_cr2"))`, on `r fmt_num(bailout_of("bailout", "df_cr2"), 1)` df |
| the other 19 | +`r fmt_num(bailout_of("other", "b"), 5)` | `r fmt_num(bailout_of("other", "p_cr2"))` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
An exclusion is a claim about **who the finding is meant to be about**, and so it is a question about the estimand. The workshop shows these samples beside the curve, as displays of how the association varies, rather than on it.
:::

::: notes
The curve uses all twenty-seven countries over the whole decade, and each restriction on this slide answers a different question, so the restrictions sit beside the curve as displays rather than on it. Splitting the decade into 2004 to 2008 and 2009 to 2013 changes the population that the claim is about, since the earlier window contains no crisis and the later one loses the comparison with the years before it. [advance] In both halves the slope of the reproduced specification is steeper than on the full panel, and its CR2 p is lower in the crisis years and about the same in the years before them. In the eight countries under an assistance programme the slope is negative, with a CR2 p of about point zero two on fewer than five degrees of freedom, and in the other nineteen it is slightly positive and far from significant. [advance] An exclusion is a claim about whom the finding is meant to describe, which makes it a question about the estimand.
:::

## Weights {#weights-whose-country-year-counts-more .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Each cell is a mean of very different numbers of respondents. Weighting by `n_cy` makes a cell built from 2,000 people count for more than one built from 500.

- **Unweighted** – every country-year is one observation. You are studying *countries*
- **Weighted by `n_cy`** – cells count in proportion to the people behind them. You are closer to studying *people*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
That changes the estimand, so whose average counts is one of the seven decisions about the question. The curve counts every country-year once. Weighted by respondents, `r fmt_pct(dev_of("n_cell"))` of its twins lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, and weighted by adult population `r fmt_pct(dev_of("pop"))`, against `r fmt_pct(share_sig(spec_curve))` on the curve.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The population weight answers another question, about the average European rather than the average member state.
:::

::: notes
Each cell of the panel is a mean over a very different number of respondents, so weighting by that count makes a country-year built from two thousand people count for more than one built from five hundred. The weighting sounds like a technical refinement, but it changes what you study. Unweighted, every country-year is one observation and you study countries, with Malta counting as much as Germany, whereas weighted, cells count in proportion to the people behind them, which moves you a long way towards studying people. That is a change of estimand, which is why the workshop treats the weighting as one of the decisions about the question rather than as an argument of the fitting function. [advance] The curve counts every country-year once, because the claim is about countries. Weighted by respondents, the share of specifications that clear the CR2 test falls from about seventy-seven per cent to about sixty-five, and weighted by adult population it falls to a quarter. [advance] The population weight is a fair choice for a different question, about the average European rather than the average member state.
:::

## Making the axes comparable {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
A coefficient on a share and one on a count, or one from a model of country-years and one from a model of respondents, are not on the same scale. The robustness study and this workshop put them on one scale in three steps:

- Take the test statistic and the degrees of freedom of its fit
- Convert to a **partial correlation** *r* – the association between predictor and outcome, net of everything else in the model, on a fixed −1 to +1 scale
- Apply **claim alignment**, so the sign means the same thing everywhere
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The df must count the units that carry the evidence. Fed the clustered *t* of the reproduced specification on 26 df, the formula returns *r* = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr1_g1", "r_formula"))` in place of `r fmt_num(curve_ref$r)` with the estimate unchanged, so the curve, and every class submission, takes its height from the conventional fit and its class from the CR2 test.
:::

::: notes
The conversion puts every result on the class chart. A coefficient on a share and one on a count, or one from a model of respondents and one from a model of country-years, are not on the same scale, so an axis that holds both would mean nothing. The robustness study, and the workshop after it, take the test statistic and its degrees of freedom, convert them to a partial correlation, and apply claim alignment, so that the sign means the same thing everywhere. [advance] The conversion is only as good as its degrees of freedom. Fed the clustered t of my specification on twenty-six degrees of freedom, it returns minus point four one where the conventional fit gives minus point two four, a larger number from weaker evidence. The curve and your submissions therefore take their height from the conventional fit and their class from the CR2 test, and `submit_exploration()` and `report_result()` send that pair for you.
:::
